patriotic rhetoric: Intensity of explicit celebration of the United States—its history, symbols, and national virtues. High ratings go to speeches thick with praise for American greatness, exceptionalism, flag imagery, and calls to unity under national ideals. Low ratings apply when patriotism is muted or expressed only in perfunctory ceremonial lines.
foreign policy focus: Degree to which international relations, alliances, conflicts, or global trade dominate the agenda. High ratings reflect sustained discussion of foreign leaders, wars, diplomacy, or global crises presented as core national concerns. Low ratings indicate only brief or ceremonial mentions of world affairs.
supportive of rugged individualism: Emphasis on self-reliance, personal responsibility, and limited government intervention. High ratings are given when speeches glorify entrepreneurship, frontier spirit, and citizens solving problems without state help. Low ratings apply when collective action and government programs are foregrounded instead.
pro welfare state: Strength of advocacy for expansive government social programs—universal health care, social security, housing, or income support. High ratings go to speeches championing new benefits or major expansions of safety-net spending. Low ratings occur when welfare programs are criticized or barely mentioned.
populist: Use of people-versus-elite framing that casts ordinary citizens against entrenched power. High ratings mark frequent attacks on political insiders, big corporations, or media elites and calls to return power to ‘the people.’ Low ratings reflect technocratic or consensus-seeking tone with little anti-elite language.
anger towards other party: Open hostility or sharp blame aimed at the opposing political party. High ratings are given when speeches single out the rival party by name, accuse it of sabotage, or use inflammatory descriptors. Low ratings apply when partisan references are absent or conciliatory.
religious rhetoric: Frequency and prominence of explicit references to God, scripture, prayer, or divine mission. High ratings indicate repeated invocations of faith as a source of authority or national purpose. Low ratings occur when religion is absent or confined to generic blessings.
isolationist: Preference for limiting U.S. engagement abroad—opposing military interventions, foreign aid, or entangling alliances. High ratings are assigned when speeches stress staying out of foreign conflicts and prioritizing domestic needs. Low ratings apply when international leadership and alliances are championed.
institutionalist: Degree of respect for constitutional norms, checks and balances, and established government processes. High ratings correspond to speeches praising Congress, courts, or the rule of law and urging bipartisan cooperation. Low ratings apply when institutions are disparaged as corrupt, weak, or obstacles to the people’s will.
optimistic about technological progress: Level of positive framing of science and technology as engines of future prosperity and national strength. High ratings go to speeches envisioning breakthroughs, pledging research investment, or celebrating innovation as a patriotic mission. Low ratings occur when technology is treated cautiously, ignored, or framed mainly as a threat.
